title: Meta-Learning Preferences for Multilingual LLM Alignment
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Meta-training on data-rich source tasks, then fine-tuning on a tiny target set, beats baselines that train on target data alone.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; two parallel pipeline rows, results bars at right
description: A left-to-right flow diagram in four zones. On the left, a gray panel titled 'Source Preference Data' holds three cards for English, French and Italian. Each card shows a preferred sample (green check) and a rejected one (red cross). Arrows lead into two parallel rows. The top row is green: MAML-DPO (meta-train), then Adaptation-DPO (few-shot fine-tune), then a dark green MAML-DPO Policy. The bottom row is purple: MAML-RLHF, Adaptation-RLHF, then MAML-RLHF Policy. An orange box in the center, 'Target Language: Romanian (~100 samples)', feeds up and down into both adaptation stages. On the right, a 'Performance on target (Romanian)' panel shows horizontal bars. Each MAML policy bar is long and colored. Each baseline bar is short and red.
caption: When the target language has low resource availability (e.g. Romanian) and has a very small number of data samples, such as 100, conventional approaches fail to properly fine-tune LLMs. On the other hand, our approach first meta-trains the model using other languages with sufficient data, allowing the model to boost sample efficiency in the target language. Our MAML-DPO/MAML-RLHF methods achieve significant performance improvement over the baseline methods, given the same amount of datapoints from the target language.
abstract: Unequal availability of human preference data across languages poses a significant challenge for aligning large language models in multilingual settings. To address the lack of sufficient data in low-resource language alignment, we propose a meta-learning framework for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Direct Preference Optimization. By leveraging preference data from other languages, our framework learns a transferable initialization that enables effective adaptation to a target language with minimal data. We provide theoretical guarantees for both the meta-reward modeling and meta-policy optimization settings, and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on multilingual benchmarks. In an extremely low-resource setting with only 100 target-language preference samples, our approach achieves up to $33.4\%$ win-rate improvements over baseline methods, and consistently outperforms baselines across multiple target languages and model scales. Our approaches retain these advantages across different combinations of meta-training languages and varying linguistic distances from the target languages.
